title: The Unquiet Inheritance
premise: When Beatrix Dunmore, the reclusive coroner of Hollow Creek, is handed a missing-persons file for Lila Voss, she notices something impossible: entries in Lila's recovered diary continue three weeks past her disappearance. Following the diary's coded references to the town's founding families, Beatrix uncovers a decades-old cover-up of a mill disaster that killed eleven workers, with her own late father among those who signed the silence order. The 'dead witness' is Lila herself, hiding in the flooded mine tunnels beneath the town, protected by an aging former sheriff who faked her death to keep her testimony alive. In the climax, Beatrix must choose between exposing the conspiracy—including her father's complicity—and preserving the fragile peace of a town built on its own buried dead; she chooses justice, testifying alongside Lila as the mill heirs are finally named.
about_author: Theo Blackwood is the pen name of a former rural paramedic who spent fifteen years responding to calls in towns too small for their own police force. They write mysteries about the quiet violence hidden inside close-knit communities.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix Dunmore, POV. Beatrix catalogs another 'accidental' death—a drowned drifter whose lungs hold no water—and quietly adds him to her private ledger of mislabeled deaths. The emotional beat is weary competence: she knows this town better than it knows itself, and it has never once thanked her for it.

chapters.title: A Diary That Outlived Its Owner
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Sheriff's deputy Ren Okafor brings her the Voss case: Lila, missing six weeks, presumed fled or dead. Beatrix reads the recovered diary and finds entries dated after the disappearance—shaky handwriting describing 'the tunnels' and 'the man who counts the graves.' The beat is cold dread blooming into obsession.

chapters.title: What the Mill Remembered
chapters.summary: Beatrix and Ren alternate POV. Digging through county archives, they connect Lila's coded dates to the 1979 Hollis Mill collapse that killed eleven workers—officially ruled structural failure. Beatrix finds her father's signature on the settlement documents. The beat is betrayal surfacing like a body in spring thaw.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears She's Dead
chapters.summary: Ren, POV. Ren canvasses the town and finds a wall of polite denial: the mill heirs—the Ashcombe family—own half of Hollow Creek, and everyone repeats the same rehearsed line about Lila being unstable. Someone slashes Beatrix's tires and leaves a funeral wreath on her porch. The beat is isolation sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts the Graves
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. The diary phrase leads Beatrix to Ezra Pike, the retired groundskeeper of the pauper's cemetery, who once worked the mill. He admits he helped stage Lila's death with former Sheriff Dale Merrick—but refuses to say where she is, warning that two people who asked before are now in Beatrix's ledger. The beat is fear wearing the mask of loyalty.

chapters.title: Water Under Stone
chapters.summary: Ren, POV. Ren discovers the drowned drifter from chapter one was a private investigator hired by one of the Ashcombe heirs to find Lila first—and silence her. Meanwhile Beatrix deciphers the diary's final entry: coordinates pointing beneath the old mill ruins. The beat is the race becoming explicit, the hunters now hunted.

chapters.title: Into the Flooded Dark
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Beatrix descends alone into the abandoned mine tunnels at night, following Lila's markers through knee-deep water. She finds the camp—recently abandoned, still warm—and a second diary detailing everything Lila witnessed the night of the collapse cover-up's modern echo: the heirs burning records. The beat is claustrophobic hope.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Father's Name
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Cornered by Ashcombe men at the tunnel mouth, Beatrix is saved by Ezra and Dale, who finally reveal Lila's location—but only if Beatrix agrees to keep her hidden until the grand jury convenes. Reading her father's letters, Beatrix learns he signed under threat but kept evidence against the heirs. The beat is grief reconciled with resolve.

chapters.title: Eleven Bells
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. On the anniversary of the collapse, the heirs move to destroy the mine entrance—with Lila still inside. Beatrix triggers the church bells, drawing the whole town to the ruins, and forces the confrontation into daylight: Lila emerges alive before hundreds of witnesses no one can silence. The beat is cathartic exposure.

chapters.title: Graves With Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Months later, the heirs stand indicted, the eleven victims' names are carved into a new memorial, and Beatrix closes her private ledger—every death accounted for, every grave given back its name. She and Ren plant a rosemary bush over her father's plot. The beat is belonging earned, not inherited.
